松平定敬.note: Lord of the Kuwana domain in Ise and, from 1864, Kyoto Shoshidai. He was the younger brother of the Kyoto Protector Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the two chief security offices of the capital were thus held by one family.

神保内蔵助.note: An elder councillor (karō) of the Aizu domain and its senior officer on the Kyoto command; full name Jinbō Kuranosuke Toshitaka. He would be made to take his own life in 1868, blamed for the Aizu retreat at Toba-Fushimi.

真木和泉守.note: Maki Izumi (Yasuomi), a Shinto priest of Kurume and the most radical strategist of the loyalist cause; a chief planner of Chōshū's march on Kyoto. He died on Tennōzan (ch. 25).

福原越後.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) who led the Fushimi wing of the 1864 expedition. Wounded in the fighting, he was afterward ordered by his own domain to commit seppuku as one of the three councillors held responsible for the defeat.

来島又兵衛.note: A Chōshū warrior famed for his valor, given command of the Saga (Tenryū-ji) force. He was killed at the Hamaguri Gate (ch. 25).

国司信濃.note: A young Chōshū elder councillor (karō), only twenty-five, given overall field command of the Kyoto expedition. He was ordered to commit seppuku after the defeat.

福田理兵衛.note: A loyalist country samurai (gōshi) of Shimo-Saga who had earlier arranged the billeting of Chōshū troops at the Tenryū-ji. Romanization mine.

天竜寺.note: A great Rinzai Zen monastery in Saga, in the western reaches of Kyoto, head temple of its own branch; founded in 1339 to placate the spirit of the late Emperor Go-Daigo. Its walled compound made a natural fortress.

蛤御門.note: The Hamaguri-gomon, the 'Clam Gate,' one of the gates in the wall enclosing the Kyoto Imperial Palace. The battle about to be fought here gave the whole affair its name: the Hamaguri Gate Incident (Kinmon no Hen).

天王山.note: A hill commanding the Yamazaki defile on the road between Kyoto and Osaka, proverbial in Japanese for a decisive position. Maki Izumi and his men made their last stand here.

黒谷.note: The Kurodani precinct (the temple Konkai Kōmyō-ji), on the eastern hills of Kyoto, which served as the Aizu domain's Kyoto headquarters.

三田尻.note: Chōshū's chief port on the Inland Sea, in Suō province (the modern Hōfu), from which the domain shipped its expeditionary force toward Osaka.

ch24.note: In the shogun’s own capital, arrests fell to the yoriki and their dōshin — mounted and foot constables under the town magistrate. They were direct shogunal subordinates, yet hereditary petty officials, ranked with the gokenin (low retainers without the right of audience before the shogun) and shut out of the field service that was a warrior’s honor. Because their work handled blood, corpses, and the execution ground, warrior society counted it ritually polluting and scorned them as “defiling officials.” To offer Kondō — who styled himself a loyalist swordsman — the rank of “senior yoriki” was to file the Shinsengumi under police rather than soldiers, and that is the slight that galls him here.

Lord of Kuwana and, from 1864, Kyoto Shoshidai (the deputy who governed the capital under the Protector). He and the Kyoto Protector, Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu, were brothers, both sons of the Takasu house, so the two great security offices of Kyoto sat in one family. With Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu (ch. 28) they formed the shogunal-loyalist party later nicknamed the “Ichi-Kai-Sō.”

An obsolete bronze muzzle-loader: powder and a solid iron ball were rammed home, the ball first heated red so as to set fire to whatever it struck, and touched off with a match-cord — a heated-shot field piece with a range, as Shiba says, of barely a chō (about 110 meters). The “Nirayama guns” Toshizō covets were another order of thing: modern cast cannon from the reverberatory furnace raised at Nirayama in Izu by the intendant Egawa Tarōzaemon, one of the first Western-style ordnance foundries in Japan.

In shōgi, Japanese chess, the gyoku or king is the piece a player must protect above all others; once it is taken the game is lost. Kondō casts the Emperor as that king-piece — the one counter neither side can afford to have captured — which is precisely the logic of the war now opening: whoever holds the sovereign is in the right.

Two monuments of loyalist history-writing: the Dai Nihon-shi (“History of Great Japan”), the vast chronicle begun in the seventeenth century under the Mito branch of the Tokugawa, and Rai San’yō’s Nihon Gaishi (“Unofficial History of Japan,” 1827). Both held that legitimacy descended through the imperial line, and from them came the maxim Shiba cites — that the side which holds the Emperor is by definition the kangun, the imperial army, its opponents rebels. It is why Chōshū and the shogunate alike strained to seize the sovereign’s person.

Maki Izumi (Yasuomi), 1813–1864, a Shinto priest of Kurume and the most uncompromising theorist-strategist of the revere-the-Emperor, expel-the-barbarian cause, and a chief planner of Chōshū’s advance on Kyoto. When it failed he made his last stand on Tennōzan and died there by his own hand with sixteen companions (ch. 25).

ch24.anchor: the Hamaguri Gate of the palace
ch24.note: The Hamaguri-gomon, the “Clam Gate,” one of the gates in the wall that enclosed the Kyoto Imperial Palace. By tradition it was so named because, like a clam that opens only in fire, it had once been forced open by a great blaze after standing shut for years. The battle about to be fought at it gave the affair its lasting name: the Hamaguri Gate Incident (Kinmon no Hen) of 1864.
